Comparing the dataset with SAG

Source: vignettes/articles/compare-with-sag.Rmd
compare-with-sag.Rmd

The official results of an ICES stock assessment are the summary tables in the ICES Stock Assessment Graphs database, SAG: spawning stock biomass, fishing pressure, recruitment and catches by year. The dataset holds the detail behind those tables, the numbers, weights, maturity and mortality by age. If a submitted stock object really is the assessment that the advice was based on, the summary calculated from it should be the same as the summary in SAG.

This article makes that comparison, for one stock and then for all of them, using the icesSAG package to read SAG and the FLCore package to calculate the summary. It is run against the live SAG database each time this site is built, so the results change as assessments are published or corrected.

Code 
library(FLStockpile)
library(FLCore)
library(icesSAG)
library(ggplot2)

options(FLStockpile.url = "https://github.com/neilcampbelll/FLstockpile/releases/download/v2026.001")

Summary of a stock

The summary of a stock in the dataset is calculated from its FLStock object. The spawning stock biomass, mean fishing mortality and recruitment come from the model estimates. The catches in SAG are usually the observed catches, so the catches come from the observed data where the dataset has them, and from the estimates otherwise.

Code 
# The summary of a stock assessment in the dataset.
#
# Returns a data frame with one row per quantity and year.

dataset_summary <- function(stock_code, assessment_year) {
  estimated <- stockpile_flstock(stock_code, assessment_year, type = "estimated")
  version <- stockpile_stocks(stock_code, assessment_year)
  catches <- if (version$observed) {
    catch(stockpile_flstock(stock_code, assessment_year, type = "observed"))
  } else {
    catch(estimated)
  }

  quantities <- list(SSB = ssb(estimated), F = fbar(estimated), recruitment = rec(estimated), catches = catches)
  rows <- lapply(names(quantities), function(quantity) {
    values <- as.data.frame(quantities[[quantity]])
    data.frame(quantity = quantity, year = values$year, dataset = values$data)
  })
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}

# The summary of a stock assessment in SAG, in the same layout.

sag_summary <- function(stock_code, assessment_year) {
  sag <- getSAG(stock_code, assessment_year)
  rows <- lapply(c("SSB", "F", "recruitment", "catches"), function(quantity) {
    data.frame(quantity = quantity, year = sag$Year, sag = sag[[quantity]])
  })
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}

# The two summaries side by side, for the years and quantities in both.

compare_summaries <- function(stock_code, assessment_year) {
  both <- merge(dataset_summary(stock_code, assessment_year), sag_summary(stock_code, assessment_year))
  both <- both[!is.na(both$dataset) & !is.na(both$sag) & both$sag != 0, ]
  both$ratio <- both$dataset / both$sag
  both[order(both$quantity, both$year), ]
}

One stock

Sole in the eastern English Channel, sol.27.7d, has both observed data and model estimates in the dataset.

Code 
sole <- compare_summaries("sol.27.7d", 2026)
tail(sole[sole$quantity == "SSB", ], 5)
#>     quantity year   dataset   sag     ratio

#> 174      SSB 2023 10193.933 10194 0.9999934

ggplot(sole, aes(year)) +

The largest difference, in any year, for each quantity:

Code 
aggregate(ratio ~ quantity, sole, function(ratio) max(abs(ratio - 1)))
#>      quantity        ratio
#> 1     catches 3.932854e-04
#> 2           F 2.117354e-03
#> 3 recruitment 3.755920e-05
#> 4         SSB 3.979648e-05

All stocks

The same comparison is made for the latest version of every stock assessment in the dataset that has model estimates. Stocks with more than one season, unit or area are left out, because their summary cannot be calculated in the same simple way, and so are stocks that are not found in SAG.

Code 
stocks <- stockpile_stocks()
stocks <- stocks[stocks$estimated, ]
stocks$simple <- stocks$n_seasons == 1 & stocks$n_units == 1 & stocks$n_areas == 1

comparisons <- lapply(which(stocks$simple), function(i) {
  compared <- try(compare_summaries(stocks$stock_code[i], stocks$assessment_year[i]), silent = TRUE)
  if (inherits(compared, "try-error") || nrow(compared) == 0) {
    return(NULL)
  }
  cbind(stock_code = stocks$stock_code[i], assessment_year = stocks$assessment_year[i], compared)
})
comparisons <- do.call(rbind, comparisons)

stocks$compared <- paste(stocks$stock_code, stocks$assessment_year) %in%
  paste(comparisons$stock_code, comparisons$assessment_year)

Of the 43 stock assessments with estimates, 36 could be compared with SAG. Not compared because they have seasons, units or areas: pra.27.3a4a, san.sa.1r, san.sa.2r, san.sa.3r. Not found in SAG: meg.27.7b-k8abd, nep.fu.32, whg.27.6a.

A stock and quantity is taken to be the same in the dataset and in SAG if they are within 2.5% of each other in every year. SAG holds rounded values, so small differences are expected: a fishing mortality of 0.02 held to three decimal places can be 2.5% out.

Code 
agreement <- aggregate(
  ratio ~ stock_code + assessment_year + quantity, comparisons,
  function(ratio) max(abs(ratio - 1)) < 0.025
)
names(agreement)[4] <- "same"

table(agreement$quantity, ifelse(agreement$same, "same", "different"))
#>              
#>               different same
#>   catches            14   12
#>   F                   7   29
#>   recruitment         7   27
#>   SSB                 5   31
Code 
all_same <- aggregate(same ~ stock_code + assessment_year, agreement, all)

15 of the 36 stock assessments are the same as SAG in every quantity that could be compared.

Explore a stock

Choose a stock to see its summary in the dataset and in SAG, as a plot and as a table. The points are the SAG values and the lines the dataset values.

Code 
library(plotly)
library(crosstalk)
library(DT)

# one row per stock and year, with the dataset and SAG value of each quantity
explore <- comparisons[c("year", "quantity", "dataset", "sag")]
explore$stock <- paste(comparisons$stock_code, comparisons$assessment_year)
explore <- reshape(explore, idvar = c("stock", "year"), timevar = "quantity", direction = "wide")
explore <- explore[order(explore$stock, explore$year), ]

shared <- SharedData$new(explore, key = ~ paste(stock, year))

# the plot of one quantity
panel <- function(quantity) {
  plot_ly(shared, x = ~year) |>
    add_markers(
      y = as.formula(paste0("~sag.", quantity)), name = "SAG", legendgroup = "SAG",
      showlegend = quantity == "SSB", marker = list(color = "#d95f02")
    ) |>
    add_lines(
      y = as.formula(paste0("~dataset.", quantity)), name = "dataset", legendgroup = "dataset",
      showlegend = quantity == "SSB", line = list(color = "#1b9e77")
    ) |>
    layout(
      yaxis = list(rangemode = "tozero", title = quantity),
      xaxis = list(title = "")
    )
}

quantities <- c("SSB", "F", "recruitment", "catches")
values <- c(rbind(paste0("dataset.", quantities), paste0("sag.", quantities)))
Code 
subplot(lapply(quantities, panel), nrows = 2, shareX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE, margin = 0.06) |>
  layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.1)) |>
  config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
Code 
datatable(
  shared,
  rownames = FALSE,
  style = "bootstrap5",
  class = "compact stripe",
  colnames = c("stock", "year", gsub(".", " ", values, fixed = TRUE)),
  options = list(
    columnDefs = list(list(targets = 0, visible = FALSE)),
    order = list(list(1, "desc")),
    pageLength = 10,
    dom = "tip"
  )
) |>
  formatSignif(values, digits = 4)

Where they differ

For each stock and quantity that is not the same, the median over the years of the dataset value divided by the SAG value, and the range. A blank means the quantity is the same, and - that it could not be compared.

Code 
ratios <- aggregate(
  ratio ~ stock_code + assessment_year + quantity, comparisons,
  function(ratio) {
    if (max(abs(ratio - 1)) < 0.025) {
      ""
    } else {
      sprintf("%s (%s to %s)", signif(median(ratio), 3), signif(min(ratio), 3), signif(max(ratio), 3))
    }
  }
)
ratios <- reshape(ratios, idvar = c("stock_code", "assessment_year"), timevar = "quantity", direction = "wide")
names(ratios) <- sub("ratio.", "", names(ratios), fixed = TRUE)
ratios[is.na(ratios)] <- "-"
ratios <- ratios[rowSums(ratios[-(1:2)] != "" & ratios[-(1:2)] != "-") > 0, ]

knitr::kable(ratios[order(ratios$stock_code), ], row.names = FALSE)

There are several reasons for a difference, and most of them are not errors:

  • Catches. The dataset catches are the estimates where no observed data were submitted, and SAG usually has the observed catches. A median close to 1 with a range around it is what that looks like.
  • Units. SAG may hold a quantity in different units, for example recruitment in millions against thousands in the stock object, giving a ratio of 0.001 or 1000.
  • Relative quantities. For some stocks SAG holds the biomass and fishing pressure relative to a reference point, such as B/BMSY, or a harvest rate in place of a fishing mortality. The description of each quantity is in the stockSizeDescription and fishingPressureDescription columns of getSAG().
  • Definitions. The spawning stock biomass or recruitment published may be defined differently from the standard calculation used here, for example at another time of year or at another age.
  • A different assessment. If none of these apply, the submitted stock object may not be the assessment that was published.

The stocks compared, with how SAG describes their quantities:

Code 
descriptions <- lapply(which(stocks$compared), function(i) {
  sag <- getSAG(stocks$stock_code[i], stocks$assessment_year[i])
  data.frame(
    stock_code = stocks$stock_code[i],
    assessment_year = stocks$assessment_year[i],
    stock_size = sag$stockSizeDescription[1],
    stock_size_units = sag$stockSizeUnits[1],
    fishing_pressure = sag$fishingPressureDescription[1],
    recruitment_age = sag$recruitment_age[1]
  )
})
